January was wetter than normal across much of South Central Texas. A large part of the central and western sections of the region had 150 percent of normal or higher rainfall during the month. This meant 13 counties improved to better than severe category drought (D0-D1). Only in Kinney, Dimmit, and Maverick Counties did the drought worsen during January. Fire danger was moderate to very high across the region. Seven of the 14 counties in severe drought (D2) or worse had burn bans in effect: Dimmit, Edwards, Karnes, Kinney, Llano, Maverick, and Val Verde. Area lakes and reservoirs continued below normal pool elevations with Lake Amistad around 44 feet below normal, Lake Travis near 50 feet below normal, and Medina Lake 74 feet below normal which left the lake at 8.8 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer showed some increase, but was still 16.2 feet below normal, and just over 3 feet below the level in January 2012. Uvalde was in stage 3 water restrictions, Austin was in stage 2 water restrictions, and Kerrville and San Marcos were in Stage 1 water restrictions.

February was another dry month across most of South Central Texas. Twenty-six of the 33 counties received 25 percent or less of their average rainfall for the month. Only Karnes and parts of Atascosa and DeWitt received near or above normal rain. As a result, the drought worsened in 15 counties. Kinney and Val Verde moved into the exceptional category (Stage D4), Hays and Maverick to extreme (D3), and Bandera, Blanco, Caldwell, Comal, Fayette, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Kendall, Lee, Travis, and Zavala to severe (D2). The rest of the counties in South Central Texas were unchanged from January. Fire danger was moderate to very high across the region. Of the 26 counties in D2 or worse drought 16 had outdoor burn bans if effect at the end of the month. These were Blanco, Caldwell, Dimmit, Edwards, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Kendall, Kerr, Kinney, Llano, Maverick, Travis, Uvalde, Val Verde, and Williamson. The Texas Crop and Weather Report issued by Texas A and M Agricultural reported rangeland and pastures continued to deteriorate. Wheat and oats badly needed rain. Ranchers continued supplemental feeding of livestock. Small trees and brush were budding, but growth was slow and weak. Area lakes and reservoirs continued below normal pool elevations with Lake Amistad around 51 feet below normal, Lake Travis near 50 feet below normal, and Medina Lake 77 feet below normal which left the lake at 7.5 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer was 20.3 feet below normal, and just over 17 feet below the level at the end of February 2012. Uvalde was in stage 3 water restrictions, Austin, the San Antonio Water System, and the Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District were in stage 2 water restrictions, and Kerrville and San Marcos were in Stage 1 restrictions.

Area lakes and reservoirs continued below normal pool elevations with Lake Amistad around 51 feet below normal, Lake Travis near 50 feet below normal, and Medina Lake 77 feet below normal which left the lake at 7.5 percent of capacity. Uvalde was in stage 3 water restrictions, Austin, the San Antonio Water System, and the Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District were in stage 2 water restrictions, and Kerrville and San Marcos were in Stage 1 restrictions.

March was another dry month across South Central Texas. Most of the region received less than normal rainfall with most of the southern and western areas getting less than 25 percent of normal. In addition to the dry month, March ended a dry six month period from October 2012 through March 2013. These six months ranked in the ten driest October to March periods at Del Rio, Austin Camp Mabry, and Austin Bergstrom International Airport. As a result, the drought worsened in 13 counties and only Atascosa and Frio Counties remained in better than severe category (D2) drought. Maverick County moved into the exceptional category (Stage D4), Bastrop, Caldwell, Dimmit, Fayette, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Williamson, and Zavala to extreme (D3), and Bexar, Lavaca, Medina, and Wilson to severe (D2). Edwards, Kinney and Val Verde remained in exceptional, Hays, Kerr, and Real in extreme, and Bandera, Blanco, Burnet, Comal, De Witt, Gillespie, Karnes, and Kendall in severe. Fire danger at the end of the month was low to moderate due to rain toward the end of March. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought 14 had outdoor burn bans if effect at the end of the month. These were Bexar, Dimmit, Edwards, Guadalupe, Hays, Karnes, Kendall, Kinney, Maverick, Medina, Travis, Uvalde, Val Verde, and Wilson. The Texas Crop and Weather Report issued by Texas A and M Agricultural indicated soil moisture was a problem in dry land corn, sorghum, and cotton. Area lakes and reservoirs continued below normal pool elevations with Lake Amistad around 52 feet below normal, Lake Travis 50 feet below normal, and Medina Lake nearly 80 feet below normal which left it at 6.5 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer was 19.9 feet below normal, and 4.7 feet below the level at the end of March 2012. San Marcos moved to stage 2 water restrictions. Uvalde was in stage 3 water restrictions, Austin, the San Antonio Water System, and the Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District were in stage 2, and Kerrville was in stage 1 restrictions.

April brought some much needed rain to South Central Texas. Most of the eastern half of the area received 150% or more of normal rainfall and only Kinney, Maverick, and Zavala Counties got less than 25% of normal. This rain had a mixed impact on the drought. Edwards (Stage D3), Bastrop (D2), Caldwell (D2), Fayette (D2), and Gonzales (D2) Counties each improved a category. At the same time, Bandera, Comal, Medina, and Uvalde Counties all worsened to Stage D3 and Frio County moved into the D2 stage. Kinney, Maverick, and Val Verde Counties remained in Stage D4. Dimmit, Guadalupe, Hays, Kerr, Real, Williamson, and Zavala Counties remained in Stage D3. Bexar, Blanco, Burnet, De Witt, Gillespie, Karnes, Kendall, Lavaca, Lee, Llano, Travis, and Wilson Counties remained in Stage D2. Fire danger at the end of the month was moderate to high. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought 11 had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. These were Bexar, Comal, Dimmit, Edwards, Frio, Karnes, Kinney, Maverick, Medina, Val Verde, and Wilson. The Texas Crop and Weather Report issued by Texas A and M Agricultural indicated livestock producers were supplying supplemental feed and de-stocking as necessary. The seven day stream flow averages were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Colorado, Guadalupe, Nueces, and Frio River basins. The Rio Grande basin was reporting below normal (10 to 24 percent) flow. Area lakes and reservoirs continued below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad was around 60 feet below normal at 1056.9 feet which is a new record low for the lake. Lake Travis was 52 feet below normal and Medina Lake near 82 feet below normal which left it at 5.5 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer saw some improvement from the rain in April, but was still 18.4 feet below normal, and 13.5 feet below the level at the end of April 2012. Uvalde moved into stage 5 water restrictions and the Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District into stage 3. San Marcos, Austin, and the San Antonio Water System, were in stage 2, and Kerrville was in stage 1 restrictions.

At the same time, Bandera, Comal, Medina, and Uvalde Counties all worsened to Stage D3 and Frio County moved into the D2 stage. Kinney, Maverick, and Val Verde Counties remained in Stage D4. Dimmit, Guadalupe, Hays, Kerr, Real, Williamson, and Zavala Counties remained in Stage D3. Bexar, Blanco, Burnet, De Witt, Gillespie, Karnes, Kendall, Lavaca, Lee, Llano, Travis, and Wilson Counties remained in Stage D2. Fire danger at the end of the month was moderate to high. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought 11 had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. These were Bexar, Comal, Dimmit, Edwards, Frio, Karnes, Kinney, Maverick, Medina, Val Verde, and Wilson. The Texas Crop and Weather Report issued by Texas A and M Agricultural indicated livestock producers were supplying supplemental feed and de-stocking as necessary. The seven day stream flow averages were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Colorado, Guadalupe, Nueces, and Frio River basins. The Rio Grande basin was reporting below normal (10 to 24 percent) flow. Area lakes and reservoirs continued below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad was around 60 feet below normal at 1056.9 feet which is a new record low for the lake. Lake Travis was 52 feet below normal and Medina Lake near 82 feet below normal which left it at 5.5 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer saw some improvement from the rain in April, but was still 18.4 feet below normal, and 13.5 feet below the level at the end of April 2012. Uvalde moved into stage 5 water restrictions and the Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District into stage 3. San Marcos, Austin, and the San Antonio Water System, were in stage 2, and Kerrville was in stage 1 restrictions.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in and around San Antonio and Bexar County. There was record rainfall in the San Antonio area with the San Antonio International Airport recording 9.87 inches of rain (2nd highest 24 hr total on record) and CoCoRAHS observers reporting over 11 inches.  Most of the rain fell in about six hours with four inches in one hour between 6 and 7 AM. A USGS stream and rain gauge on Olmos Creek and Dresden Drive reported 2.58 inches in 15 min between 615 and 630 am.  The gauge reported 6.13 inches in one hour, 9.46 inches in 2 hours, and totaled 15.31 inches in 5 hours.  A 24hr total at this gauge was 17 inches of rain.  This led to massive flooding in the Olmos Basin/Creek just inside Loop 410 near the Quarry.  Most of the flooding across the city was in north central and northwest San Antonio along and just side Loop 410. This rain came a day after another heavy rain event with parts of the city receiving over two inches. This all led to major flooding with Olmos Creek, the Medina River, Leon Creek, the San Antonio River, and Salado Creek all reaching major flood stage. There were many roads closed including Hwy 281 at Olmos Creek which remained closed for several days. At 10 AM, there was a foot of water over Ingram and Callaghan Rds. San Antonio creeks and streams saw big rises in their levels which led to additional flooding down steam in the south portion of Bexar County.  Areas that were hit the hardest included the Espada Road area near the San Antonio River and Loop 410 intersection.  A mobile home park on Plumnear Road off Leon Creek on the southwest side of the city was flooded out.  Several hundred rescues and calls for rescue occurred during the morning of the 25th.  Two fatalities occurred inside Bexar County. A woman was killed when her car was swept away in flood waters along Leon Creek at the 5800 Block of U.S Highway 90.  Another woman was killed in her car when her car was swept away in the 400 Block of Rhapsody Drive about 730 am.  In all the City of San Antonio and Bexar County Emergency Management agencies found over 350 impacted residences with 15 of those being destroyed and 27 suffering major damage.  The other residences suffered minor damages.  Most of the destroyed residences were in the Espada area along the San Antonio River in southeast Bexar County.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing Hwy 72 west of Kenedy and Hwy 181 at the Bee County line.

The brief tornado affected a dozen homes and aluminum carports in the Country Garden and Woodcreek communities of La Vernia. The tornado formed in an open field near the intersection of Woodcreek Dr. and Bluff Creek Rd. in Woodcreek. It then traveled north before dissipating. Straight line winds from the same storm produced additional damage further north along Country Gardens Rd., but damage ended just short of Bluebonnet Rd. (FM 775).  Maximum winds are estimated to be 70 mph.

The brief tornado did minor damage to homes near the intersection of Judson Rd. and Woodsrim St. in Live Oak. The stucco and wood facade of a medical building on Judson Rd. was completely pulled off. Several power poles were snapped with trees uprooted and limbs twisted off several mature Oak trees. The Northeast Methodist Hospital had damage to the air conditioning units on its roof and had some broken windows and doors. An aluminum storage shed behind one house was blown clearly over two houses before landing in the backyard of a third house.  Maximum winds are estimated to be 80 mph.

May brought some much needed rain to South Central Texas. Much of the area received above normal rainfall and 14 counties moved to better than severe (Stage D2) drought. In addition, Bandera, Kerr, Medina, Real, Uvalde, and Williamson Counties improved a category to stage D2. All the other counties stayed the same with Kinney, Maverick, and Val Verde in exceptional (Stage D4) drought category, Dimmit, Edwards, and Zavala in extreme (Stage D3), and Bastrop, De Witt, Frio, Gillespie, Lee, and Llano in severe (Stage D2) category. Fire danger at the end of the month was low to moderate. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought seven had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. These were Dimmit, Edwards, Frio, Kinney, Maverick, Medina, and Val Verde. The seven day stream flow averages were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Colorado River basin. The Guadalupe, Nueces, Rio Grande, and Frio River basins were reporting below normal (10 to 24 percent) flow. Area lakes and reservoirs continued below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad was around 61 feet below normal at 1056.3 feet which is a new record low for the lake. Lake Travis was 52 feet below normal and Medina Lake near 82 feet below normal which left it at 5.5 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer saw some improvement from the rain in May, but was still 8 feet below normal, and 4.2 feet below the level at the end of May 2012. Uvalde was in stage 5 water restrictions and Kerrville was in stage 1.

June was feast or famine for rainfall across South Central Texas. Most of the region had less than 50 percent of normal. However, the southwestern corner of the area received in excess of 150 percent of normal and parts of Maverick and Dimmit Counties had as much as four times normal. This rain allowed Kinney (now in extreme drought category, Stage D3), Dimmit (severe category, Stage D2), Maverick (D2), and Zavala (D2) Counties to improve their drought conditions. At the same time, the lack of rain led to drought conditions worsening to stage D3 in Bastrop and Lee Counties, and to stage D2 in Blanco, Burnet, Caldwell, Comal, Fayette, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Kendall, and Travis Counties. Val Verde (D4), Edwards (D3), Bandera (D2), De Witt (D2), Frio (D2), Gillespie (D2), Kerr (D2), Llano (D2), Medina (D2), Real (D2), Uvalde (D2), and Williamson (D2) Counties all remained unchanged from May. Fire danger at the end of the month was moderate. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Caldwell, Dimmit, Edwards, Fayette, Frio, Kinney, Lee, Llano, Maverick, Medina, and Val Verde had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The seven day stream flow averages were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Colorado River basin. The Upper and Middle Guadalupe, Nueces, Rio Grande, and Frio River basins were reporting below normal (10 to 24 percent) flow. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad was around 59 feet below normal. Lake Travis was 54 feet below normal and Medina Lake 83 feet below normal which left it at 5 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer was nearly 17 feet below normal, and 3.2 feet below the level at the end of June 2012. Uvalde was in stage 5 water restrictions, Austin was in stage 2, and Kerrville, San Marcos, and Seguin were in stage 1. The Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District was in stage 3 alarm drought status.

June was feast or famine for rainfall across South Central Texas. Most of the region had less than 50 percent of normal. In the 36 hours ending at 7 AM on June 15 as much as 16.65 inches of rain fell around Eagle Pass. The first report of flash flooding was at 10:30 AM on June 14 when Highway 277 from Eagle Pass to Quemado was closed and water was reported to be entering some homes in Eagle Pass. A short time later El Indo Hwy was closed at Memo Robinson Dr. As heavy rain continued overnight, there were multiple swift water rescues in Eagle Pass. At 5:08 AM on June 15 the Deer Run, Elm Creek, and La Herrdura subdivisions were evacuated by law enforcement officials.  In all 564 homes were impacted across the city of Eagle Pass and Maverick County, including 140 homes that were destroyed, the majority of which where in Maverick County just outside of the Eagle Pass city limits.  In addition, 143 homes had major damage and 180 homes had minor damage.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain in Kinney County with CoCoRAHS observers reporting 8.25 inches in Spofford and up to 8.05 inches in Brackettville. This rain led to flash flooding in Brackettville, Spofford, and Alamo Village. Many roads were reported closed including FM1572, FM1693, FM1908, and RM674. Barricades were placed on Fulton and Beaumont Sts. in Brackettville. Las Moras Creek overflowed in the Fort Clark Springs community.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Carrizo Springs. Several vehicles were stuck in high water at San Pedro Ave. and 3rd St.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Crystal City. A vehicle was stranded by high water at Refugio St. In addition, Wagoner Rd. on the southeast side of town was closed.
A brief tornado produced some tree and roof damage. Winds were estimated to be 85 mph at the peak of the tornado.

The drought was largely unchanged in South Central Texas in July. With the exception of the northeast and a couple of small areas in the west, most of the region received near or below normal rainfall. Kinney and Bastrop Counties had enough rain to improve from extreme drought (Stage D3) to severe drought (Stage D2). Fayette and Lavaca Counties worsened one category Fayette to Stage D3 and Lavaca to Stage D2. All of the other counties remained unchanged with Val Verde in exceptional drought (Stage D4), Edwards and Lee in D3, and the remaining counties in D2. Fire danger at the end of the month was moderate. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Bastrop, Caldwell, De Witt, Dimmit, Edwards, Fayette, Frio, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Kinney, Maverick, Medina, Travis, and Val Verde had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The seven day stream flow averages were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Lower Colorado and Lower San Antonio River basins. The Lower Guadalupe, Nueces, Rio Grande, and Frio River basins reported below normal (10 to 24 percent) flow. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed some improvement from June, but was still near 56 feet below normal. Lake Travis was also at 56 feet below normal after a small increase. Medina Lake continued to be the most affected lake at 84 feet below normal which left it at 5 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer Authority declared Stage 3 water restrictions as the aquifer dropped to 23 feet below normal, and 5.1 feet below the level at the end of June 2012. This meant that large water users were required to reduce pumping by 35%. Uvalde was in stage 5 water restrictions, Fredericksburg was in stage 4, New Braunfels stage 3, Austin was in stage 2, and Kerrville, San Marcos, and Seguin were in stage 1. The Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District was in stage 3 alarm drought status.

The Lower Guadalupe, Nueces, Rio Grande, and Frio River basins reported below normal (10 to 24 percent) flow. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed some improvement from June, but was still near 56 feet below normal. Lake Travis was also at 56 feet below normal after a small increase. Medina Lake continued to be the most affected lake at 84 feet below normal which left it at 5 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer Authority declared Stage 3 water restrictions as the aquifer dropped to 23 feet below normal, and 5.1 feet below the level at the end of June 2012. This meant that large water users were required to reduce pumping by 35%. Uvalde was in stage 5 water restrictions, Fredericksburg was in stage 4, New Braunfels stage 3, Austin was in stage 2, and Kerrville, San Marcos, and Seguin were in stage 1. The Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District was in stage 3 alarm drought status.

The drought worsened across much of South Central Texas in August. With the exception of a small part of the southeast a few other isolated spots, most of the region received near or below normal rainfall. Only Edwards and Fayette Counties saw any improvement with both going from extreme drought (Stage D3) to severe (Stage D2). Atascosa, Bexar, Karnes, Llano, and Wilson Counties moved into Stage D2. Bandera, Bastrop, Caldwell, Gillespie, Guadalupe, Kendall, and Kerr Counties moved from Stage D2 to Stage D3. Val Verde remained in Stage D4, Lee in Stage D3, and Blanco, Comal, Dimmit, Frio, Gonzales, Hays, Kinney, Medina, Real, Travis, Uvalde, Williamson, and Zavala all stayed in Stage D2. Fire danger at the end of the month was low to moderate. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Atascosa, Bandera, Bastrop, Blanco, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Dimmit, Fayette, Gillespie, Gonzales, Guadalupe, Hays, Kendall, Lee, Llano, Medina, Travis, and Val Verde had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The Texas Crop and Weather Report issued by Texas A and M Agricultural indicated extremely dry conditions continued in most of the region with rangeland and pastures in poor condition. The seven day stream flow averages were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio, Colorado, and Upper Guadalupe River basins. The Nueces, Rio Grande, Lower Guadalupe, and San Antonio River basins reported below normal (10 to 24 percent) flow. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed some improvement from July, but was still near 47 feet below normal. Lake Travis was near 60 feet below normal. Medina Lake continued to be the most affected lake at 85 feet below normal which left it at 4.5 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in Stage 3 water restrictions as the aquifer dropped to 26 feet below normal, and 8.6 feet below the level at the end of July 2012. This meant that large water users were required to reduce pumping by 35%. San Marcos moved from stage 1 water restrictions from stage 3 and Kerrville went to stage 2 from stage 1. Uvalde remained in stage 5, Fredericksburg in stage 4, New Braunfels stage 3, Austin and the San Antonio Water Systme stage 2, and Seguin in stage 1. The Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District was in stage 3 alarm drought status.

The Texas Crop and Weather Report issued by Texas A and M Agricultural indicated extremely dry conditions continued in most of the region with rangeland and pastures in poor condition. The seven day stream flow averages were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio, Colorado, and Upper Guadalupe River basins. The Nueces, Rio Grande, Lower Guadalupe, and San Antonio River basins reported below normal (10 to 24 percent) flow. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed some improvement from July, but was still near 47 feet below normal. Lake Travis was near 60 feet below normal. Medina Lake continued to be the most affected lake at 85 feet below normal which left it at 4.5 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in Stage 3 water restrictions as the aquifer dropped to 26 feet below normal, and 8.6 feet below the level at the end of July 2012. This meant that large water users were required to reduce pumping by 35%. San Marcos moved from stage 1 water restrictions from stage 3 and Kerrville went to stage 2 from stage 1. Uvalde remained in stage 5, Fredericksburg in stage 4, New Braunfels stage 3, Austin and the San Antonio Water Systme stage 2, and Seguin in stage 1. The Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District was in stage 3 alarm drought status.

September brought tremendous improvement in the drought. Most of South Central Texas received above normal precipitation with a large area seeing double their average. Twenty counties moved to better than severe drought (Stage D2) and no county worsened. Val Verde County improved from exceptional (Stage D4) to extreme (Stage D3) and was the only county in that category. Bandera, Gillespie, Kendall, and Kerr improved to join Edwards, Kinney, Real, and Uvalde in Stage D2. Fire danger at the end of the month was low to moderate. None of the counties in D2 or worse drought had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The seven day stream flow averages were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio and Upper Colorado River basins. The Nueces, San Antonio, and Lower Colorado River basins reported below normal (10 to 24 percent) flow. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed improvement from August, but was still near 38 feet below normal. Lake Travis stayed steady near 60 feet below normal. Medina Lake continued to be the most affected lake at 86 feet below normal which left it at 4 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in Stage 3 water restrictions as the aquifer dropped to 28 feet below normal, and 14 feet below the level at the end of August 2012. This meant that large water users were required to reduce pumping by 35%. Uvalde remained in stage 5 water restrictions, Fredericksburg in stage 4, New Braunfels and San Marcos in stage 3, and Austin, Kerrville, and the San Antonio Water System in stage 2. The Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District was in stage 3 alarm drought status.

Thunderstorms produced an outflow boundary that moved through Burnet County with wind gusts estimated at 40 mph and caused a large tree branch to fall on a truck in Marble Falls.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 50 mph that knocked down some five to six inch diameter tree limbs near Georgetown.
Road closed at HWY 163 AND 90W with 1 to 2ft of water over roadway.
Several low lying streets across the city were flooded, including Railway at Delarosa.
Several roads were closed from South Austin Park to Battle Bend Park to Woods of Legend Oaks Park.
There was water over Highway 539 near Sutherland Springs Cemetery.

An 8 year old boy was struck by lightning on the west side of San Antonio in the evening of Thursday September 5th. He, along with another boy, was in a backyard when the lightning strike occurred. The 8 year old was taken to the hospital in critical condition and died September 7th around noon. The other boy survived.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding at FM 685 and FM1825.
Several low water crossings were flooded across Comal county due to heavy rain.
Several roads were closed in Hondo due to flooding.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding at the intersection of FM 20 and FM 621. Time is approximate.
Public reports via Twitter that tree limbs in the Grand Oaks neighborhood of South Austin were downed. Trees and limbs varied in size from 6 to 12 inches in diameter.
Thunderstorm outflow winds broke tree limbs averaging 3 to 4 inches in diameter, and blew down a power pole.

There was two feet of water over the roadway at low water crossing on Alfred Petsch Rd near the Pedernales River. The road was closed due to high water at the low water crossing at Pfiester Rd near the Pedernales River.

Despite several significant rain events during October, there was little change in the ongoing drought as most of this rain fell in counties where the drought conditions had previously improved. The only counties remaining in severe (Stage D2) or worse category were Val Verde (Stage D3), Bandera, Edwards, Gillespie, Kendall, Kerr, and Real (all in Stage D2). None of these counties saw any change in their drought category during October. Fire danger at the end of the month was low to moderate. None of the counties in D2 or worse drought had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The seven day stream flow averages were below normal (10 to 24 percent) across the Upper Nueces and Medina River basins. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed slight improvement from September, but was still near 37 feet below normal. Lake Travis rose nearly five feet, but was still more than 55 feet below normal. Medina Lake saw almost no rain and continued to be the most affected lake at 87 feet below normal which left it at 4 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer rose during the month and was up to 26 feet below normal, and 7 feet below the level at the end of October 2012. This allowed the Edwards Aquifer Authority to ease water restrictions to stage 2 requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Fredericksburg remained in stage 4 water restrictions and Kerrville was able to improve to stage 1.

Despite several significant rain events during October, there was little change in the ongoing drought as most of this rain fell in counties where the drought conditions had previously improved. The only counties remaining in severe (Stage D2) or worse category were Val Verde (Stage D3), Bandera, Edwards, Gillespie, Kendall, Kerr, and Real (all in Stage D2). None of these counties saw any change in their drought category during October. Fire danger at the end of the month was low to moderate. None of the counties in D2 or worse drought had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The seven day stream flow averages were below normal (10 to 24 percent) across the Upper Nueces and Medina River basins. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed slight improvement from September, but was still near 37 feet below normal. Lake Travis rose nearly five feet, but was still more than 55 feet below normal. Medina Lake saw almost no rain and continued to be the most affected lake at 87 feet below normal which left it at 4 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer rose during the month and was up to 26 feet below normal, and 7 feet below the level at the end of October 2012. This allowed the Edwards Aquifer Authority to ease water restrictions to stage 2 requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Fredericksburg remained in stage 4 water restrictions and Kerrville was able to improve to stage 1.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding sending one foot of water over South Hausman Rd. at a low water crossing near Helotes. The 24 hour rainfall in the area ranged from 3.02 to 4.08 inches.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding in Pflugerville. Four feet of water swept cars off Grand Avenue Parkway which necessitated two swift water rescues. A CoCoRaHS observer in the area reported 5.72 inches of rain in the 24 hours ending at 7AM.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding in Comal County. People were evacuated along River Road in New Braunfels, and near Spring Branch, Elm Creek was running 40 to 50 feet wide where it is normally about four feet. The 24 hour rainfall in the River Rd. area ranged from 3.81 to 6.58 inches while in the Spring Branch area there was between 10.40 and 11.75 inches.  A man fell into the Guadalupe River near the horseshoe just down from Canyon Dam.  The man was trying to retrieve some equipment while the river was quickly rising.  The 26 year old drown and his body was recovered a few days later.  Portions of River Road just west of New Braunfels became flooded between 1 and 2 am in the morning.
A thunderstorm produced a lightning strike that caused a structural fire.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding in Wimberley, San Marcos, Buda, and Kyle.  Public reports of 14 inches of rain fell near Wimberley and this rainfall made its way into the Blanco River Watershed and the Onion Creek Watershed.  Rainfall totals near Bude and Kyle were upwards of 8-10 inches. The Blanco River flooded and major flooding occurred downstream to San Marcos.  The Blanco River crested at 26.74 feet in Wimberley. The Blanco River USGS gauge at Kyle crested at 35.92 feet.  Flooding then occurred in the San Marcos River as the flood wave crossed I-35 and flooded areas near Martindale in Caldwell County.  Reports indicate that the Blanco River was near or slightly higher than the 1998 flood of record.  Sections of San Marcos flooded near the Blanco River including areas of Texas State University and areas along River Road where several evacuations of residences occurred.  The Blanco River was 100 feet out of its banks.  In many areas along the Blanco River, debris was found 15 to 20 feet up.  Several roads needed repair and several homes were flooded out.  Across Hays County, 47 homes sustained minor damage, 24 sustained major damage, and one home was destroyed.  Four businesses sustained major damage including the Buda Fire Department station and Buda Elementary.
A thunderstorm produced a lightning strike that caused a structural fire.
A thunderstorm produced a lightning strike that caused a structural fire.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding in Wimberley. Observers reported 12.45 to 14.01 inches of rain in the 24 hours ending at 7AM. This flooded a workshop with one half inch of water. A citizen estimated the river level near the confluence of the Blanco River and Cypress Creek was higher than that of the 1998 flood.

After a night of heavy rain, runoff into the San Marcos River sent a flood wave downstream. Below San Marcos there was flooding at the Pecan Park Campground. Farther downstream the river sent water over FM1979 closing the road, and there was a swift water rescue at FM 1977 near Staples.  There were 21 homes destroyed across Caldwell County, 20 of which were mobile homes.  Most of the homes that were damaged and destroyed were uninsured.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in the Rollingwood and Sunset Valley sections of Austin. Rainfall totals were as much as 11.33 inches in Travis County near Barton Creek and Loop 360 in west Austin. There were several high water rescues in both Rollingwood and Sunset Valley. Major flooding was reported along Williamson Creek near Heartwood Drive in south Austin.  One fatality was discovered along Williamson Creek near Heartwood drive. The fatality was a homeless man.  Several homes along Heartwood drive sustained considerable flood damage and damage was reported along Lady Bird Lake and Barton Springs Pool.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Caldwell County. Numerous roads around the county were closed due to water covering them. Rainfall totals in the county were as much as 4.02 inches.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Uvalde County. FM1051 was closed due to flooding after as much as 3.47 inches of rain fell.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Hays County. Numerous roads were closed due to flooding around Wimberley, Driftwood, Dripping Springs, Kyle, and Buda.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Crystal City. There was a high water rescue on JFK Dr. and several other roads were closed including Starr St.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Big Wells and Carrizo Springs. Parts of Highway 85 were covered with water and closed due to needed repair. Some homes in Carrizo Springs were flooded up to the window sills. A co-op observer in Carrizo Springs reported 10.65 inches and a co-op observer in Big Wells reported 9.50 inches.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Eagle Pass. Several homes were evacuated, manhole covers were blown out, roads were damaged by flood water, and several roads were closed due to flooding.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Pflugerville. Several roads and low water crossings were not passable due to rising water.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in the Austin area. Low water crossings were flooded closing Bee Caves Rd., Joe Tanner Ln., Wasson Rd., and David Moore Dr.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Dimmit County. Nearly all major roads in the county were closed due to high water including Highway 83 between Carrizo Springs and Asherton, FM1433, FM1407, FM1556, and FM468.  A CoCoRaHS observer 3.0 miles NNE of Carrizo Springs reported a rainfall total of 17.67 inches of rain during this event.  Several other rainfall totals of 11 to 13 inches were reported in the Carrizo Springs and Crystal City area.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in Dimmit County. Highway 85 was closed between Carrizo Springs and Dilley and a few stranded motorists needed assistance.
The Zavala County Emergency Manager reported street flooding in Crystal City.  A shelter was opened for displaced residents.
There was flooding reported along Barton Creek and water rescues along Bee Cave Road.

Across Round Rock and the northern sections of Williamson County, heavy rain fell much of the night with areas reporting up to 10 inches of rain.  At the peak of the flooding there were 23 areas closed due to high water. Several homes along Brushy Creek were evacuated.  Houses were damaged over the eastern portions along the Highway 79 corridor including Forest Creek, Hutto, and the County Road 123 area.  Voluntary evacuations were called for in eastern Round Rock and Hutto.  88 homes were evacuated.  Several swift water rescues were performed including 8 vehicle rescues.  Overall 19 homes were affected by flooding rains in Williamson County with overall damages hit 1.1 million dollars in uninsured losses to public infrastructure.

The Comal County Engineer's Office website reported that portions of Smithson Valley Road had nearly 3 feet of water over it in spots.  Low water crossings were flooded across other portions of Comal and Hays Counties.
There were numerous roads closed and water rescues in and around Pflugerville.  There were rainfall reports of over 8 inches of rain during the late evening hours up through 1am.
Bastrop County Emergency Management reported that there was flooding on sections of Highway 812 between State Highway 21 and Elroy Road.

Caldwell County reported several flooded roads during the morning hours including FM 1979 at the San Marcos River, Old Colony Line Road, and FM 86.  A flash flood fatality occurred near Track Road and FM 20 East when a 51 year old teacher at Smithville Junior High was driving to work and his car was swept off the road.  His body was recovered later that day.

A truck drove around a barricade at Brushy Creek on Polonia Road.  The truck became submerged and the driver was able to escape unharmed.  The passenger was not able to escape and got swept downstream. The body of the female passenger, age 57, was found more than a week later.

Heavy rains in excess of 14 inches upstream of Austin in the Onion Creek Watershed near Wimberley caused a flash flood that hit portions of South Austin in the early morning hours.  Water started to rise and flood portions of the Onion Creek area near Interstate 35 by 4-5am on the morning of the 31st and water continued to rise into the early morning hours.  USGS gauges were overtopped near Twin Creek Road and this record flood water continued to move along Onion creek, passing under I-35 and inundating several neighborhoods between I-35 and US Highway 183.  A reverse 911 was utilized by the City of Austin to help evacuate residents but flood waters rose so quickly that most residents sheltered in place and were rescued by truck and helicopter later that morning.  Those that tried to escape the flood waters via their vehicles got caught in the rising waters and this led to several fatalities.  A mother and infant son died when their SUV vehicle was swept off the Onion Creek bridge on Bluff Springs Road in the predawn hours around 430 am. Another resident in a neighborhood along Onion Creek was also found drowned as his vehicle got swept off the road and was recovered near Pleasant Valley Drive and William Cannon.  Almost 2 weeks later the body of a homeless man was found in Williamson Creek near South First Street and Heartwood.  He was presumed a flood fatality from this event.  Manual readings were performed by USGS at the Onion Creek/Highway 183 gauge site ATIT2.  The creek crested just over 40 feet at 930 am the morning of October 31st.  This was a new record height for this location and translated to about 135,000 cubic feet per second. In total across Travis County and the City of Austin, over 700 homes were damaged by the flooding, of which over 100 were destroyed.  Most of the affected homes did not have insurance and were within the 100 year flood plain of Onion Creek.  Flood recovery lasted for several weeks including debris removal. Damage estimates are still being calculated as of this writing but damages across Travis County and the City of Austin look like they will exceed 100 million dollars.

There was no change in the drought status across South Central Texas in November despite most of the region receiving less than normal rainfall. At the end of the month Val Verde County was in extreme (Stage D3) drought category. Bandera, Edwards, Gillespie, Kendall, Kerr, and Real Counties were in severe (Stage D2) drought category. Fire danger at the end of the month was low to moderate. None of the counties in D2 or worse drought had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The seven day stream flow averages were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio and Lower San Antonio River basins and below normal (10 to 24 percent) across the Guadalupe, Medina, Nueces and Upper San Antonio River basins. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed slight improvement from October, but was still near 36 feet below normal. Lake Travis continued to see improvement, but was still 53 feet below normal. Medina Lake was again the most affected lake at 87.5 feet below normal which left it at 4 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer dropped during the month and was 28 feet below normal, and 10 feet below the level at the end of November 2012. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in stage 2 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Fredericksburg remained in stage 4 water restrictions and Kerrville was in stage 1.

Freezing drizzle produced icy spots on roads, bridges, and exposed surfaces. Ice was observed on the Colorado River bridge in Bastrop.  Several accidents were reported in Elgin.  Ice was also observed at the Highway 21/71 junction and on FM713 near the Bastrop/Caldwell County line.
Light freezing drizzle was reported at the San Antonio International Airport.  Light freezing drizzle was also reported on the north side of the city with little to no impacts reported.

Light freezing drizzle was reported in portions of the county producing icy spots on roads, bridges, and exposed surfaces. Some of the roads with ice were Highway 304 and FM713 near the Bastrop/Caldwell County line.

Freezing drizzle produced icy spots on roads, bridges, and exposed surfaces. Portions of Interstate 10 was shut down due to multiple accidents between Flatonia to Schulenburg.   Ice was also observed on Highway 71 southeast of La Grange.

Later on in the evening the eastern half of the county, mainly east of Interstate 35, experienced an accumulation of freezing drizzle that produced icy spots on roads, bridges, and exposed surfaces. A small area just north of the airport experienced a dusting of snow which lead to a 25 car accident on Highway 183.

December was a dry month across South Central Texas with most of the region receiving less than normal rainfall. Fortunately, this had little effect on the drought. De Witt County was the only county that changed into a worse drought category moving into severe drought (Stage D2).  The rest of the area remained unchanged with Val Verde County in extreme (Stage D3) drought category and Bandera, Edwards, Gillespie, Kendall, Kerr, and Real Counties in severe (Stage D2) drought category. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio, Lower San Antonio, and Guadalupe River basins and below normal (10 to 24 percent) across the Medina, Nueces, Lower Colorado, and Upper San Antonio River basins. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed slight improvement from November, but was still near 36 feet below normal. Lake Travis continued to see improvement, but was near 53 feet below normal. Medina Lake was again the most affected lake at 88.3 feet below normal which left it at 4 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer rose slightly during the month and was 27 feet below normal, and 11 feet below the level at the end of December 2012. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in stage 2 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Fredericksburg remained in stage 4 water restrictions and Kerrville in stage 1.

December was a dry month across South Central Texas with most of the region receiving less than normal rainfall. Fortunately, this had little effect on the drought. De Witt County was the only county that changed into a worse drought category moving into severe drought (Stage D2).  The rest of the area remained unchanged with Val Verde County in extreme (Stage D3) drought category and Bandera, Edwards, Gillespie, Kendall, Kerr, and Real Counties in severe (Stage D2) drought category. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio, Lower San Antonio, and Guadalupe River basins and below normal (10 to 24 percent) across the Medina, Nueces, Lower Colorado, and Upper San Antonio River basins. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed slight improvement from November, but was still near 36 feet below normal. Lake Travis continued to see improvement, but was near 53 feet below normal. Medina Lake was again the most affected lake at 88.3 feet below normal which left it at 4 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer rose slightly during the month and was 27 feet below normal, and 11 feet below the level at the end of December 2012. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in stage 2 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Fredericksburg remained in stage 4 water restrictions and Kerrville in stage 1.

A transient was swept away in a drainage ditch under Interstate 35 along Little Walnut Creek.  Widespread flash flooding was not observed, but locally heavy rainfall occured in the area and lead to stronger flow in the creek.  The transient was rescued out of the water but was unconscious. A cold front brought an arctic airmass to South Central Texas January 23rd. Isentropic upglide of warm moist air over the cold surface air led to sleet, freezing rain, and snow across the area. The first report of sleet was at 4PM in Williamson County. Sleet, freezing rain, and snow spread south and west through the afternoon and evening to Edwards and Uvalde Counties in the west and Fayette and Wilson Counties in the south. There were light ice accumulations on elevated roads and bridges leading to several accidents and road closures in the Austin metro area and Bastrop. Icy bridges were also reported in New Braunfels, Elgin, and along I-10 in Fayette County.

January was a dry month across South Central Texas with most of the region receiving less than normal rainfall. All but the eastern quarter of the area had less than 25 percent of normal for the month. Fortunately, this had little effect on the drought. Gillespie (Stage D3), Burnet, Llano, and Medina (all three D2) Counties were the only ones that changed into a worse drought category.  The rest of the area remained unchanged with Val Verde County in extreme (Stage D3) drought category and Bandera, De Witt, Edwards, Kendall, Kerr, and Real Counties in severe (Stage D2) drought category. Fire danger was moderate across the area at the end of January. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Kendall, Kerr, and Llano had burn bans in effect. The Texas Crop and Weather Report issued by Texas A&M Agricultural indicated soil moisture was low and even winter weeds weren���t growing. Dryland wheat and oats were showing signs of stress. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio, Lower San Antonio, Medina, Nueces and Guadalupe River basins  and below normal (10 to 24 percent) across the Colorado and Upper San Antonio River basins. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad showed slight improvement from December, but was still near 35 feet below normal. Lake Travis remained near 53 feet below normal. Medina Lake was again the most affected lake at 88.7 feet below normal which left it at 4 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer held steady for the month and was 27 feet below normal, and 11.5 feet below the level at the end of January 2013. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in stage 2 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Fredericksburg remained in stage 4 water restrictions and Kerrville in stage 1.

February was a dry month across South Central Texas with most of the region receiving less than normal rainfall. Much of the northern and southern parts of the area had less than 25 percent of normal for the month. With the lack of rainfall Caldwell, Fayette, Gonzales, Guadalupe, and Karnes Counties entered severe drought category (Stage D2). Despite the low rainfall, Val Verde County improved from extreme (Stage D3) to severe (Stage D2) category. The rest of the area remained unchanged with Gillespie County in extreme (Stage D3) drought category and Bandera, Burnet, De Witt, Edwards, Kendall, Kerr, Llano, and Medina Counties in severe (Stage D2) drought category. Fire danger was moderate across the area at the end of February. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Gillespie, Kendall, Llano, and Val Verde had burn bans in effect. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio, Medina, Nueces and Guadalupe River basins and below normal (10 to 24 percent) across the San Antonio River basin. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad remained near 35 feet below normal and Lake Travis remained near 53 feet below normal. Medina Lake was again the most affected, but showed a small increase to 89.8 feet below normal which left it at 4 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer also had a slight improvement for the month and was 26.7 feet below normal, and 7.4 feet below the level at the end of February 2013. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in stage 2 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Fredericksburg remained in stage 4 water restrictions and Kerrville in stage 1.

Despite the low rainfall, Val Verde County improved from extreme (Stage D3) to severe (Stage D2) category. The rest of the area remained unchanged with Gillespie County in extreme (Stage D3) drought category and Bandera, Burnet, De Witt, Edwards, Kendall, Kerr, Llano, and Medina Counties in severe (Stage D2) drought category. Fire danger was moderate across the area at the end of February. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Gillespie, Kendall, Llano, and Val Verde had burn bans in effect. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio, Medina, Nueces and Guadalupe River basins and below normal (10 to 24 percent) across the San Antonio River basin. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad remained near 35 feet below normal and Lake Travis remained near 53 feet below normal. Medina Lake was again the most affected, but showed a small increase to 89.8 feet below normal which left it at 4 percent of capacity. The Edwards Aquifer also had a slight improvement for the month and was 26.7 feet below normal, and 7.4 feet below the level at the end of February 2013. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in stage 2 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Fredericksburg remained in stage 4 water restrictions and Kerrville in stage 1.

In the wake of a strong cold front, a shallow layer of cold air settled over South Central Texas. An upper level trough moved across the southern plains and caused elevated thunderstorms during the evening of March 3rd. Some of these storms produced small hail. Then isentropic upglide of warm moist air turned the precipitation frozen during the early morning hours of the 4th. The first report of freezing rain came at 12:40am in Travis County. Icy bridges and overpasses were reported in Travis, Williamson, Fayette, and Caldwell Counties. In Fayette County, county office and school openings were delayed on March 4th.

Some of South Central Texas experienced a wet March. Across the southern portion of the region they received above normal rainfall with some places getting 150 to 200 percent of normal. Unfortunately, the north central and northwestern areas had less than 25 percent of normal for the month. With the lack of rainfall Bandera, Burnet, Kerr and Llano Counties worsened to extreme drought category (Stage D3). The rest of the area remained unchanged with Gillespie County in extreme (Stage D3) drought category and Edwards, Kendall, Medina and Val Verde Counties in severe (Stage D2) drought category. Fire danger was moderate to high across the area at the end of March. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Burnet, Kendall, Kerr, Llano, and Val Verde had burn bans in effect. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio, Medina, Nueces, Colorado, and Guadalupe River basins and below normal (10 to 24 percent) across the San Antonio and Rio Grande River basins. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad remained near 35 feet below normal and Lake Travis dropped slightly to near 54 feet below normal. Medina Lake was again the most affected at 90 feet below. The Edwards Aquifer dropped again during the month and was 28 feet below normal, and 6 feet below the level at the end of March 2013. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in stage 2 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Fredericksburg moved into stage 5 water restrictions, and Kerrville remained in stage 1.

All but a very small portion of South Central Texas experienced below normal rainfall in April. Across most of the western half of the area they received less than 25 percent of normal for the month. With the lack of rainfall Edwards, Kerr, Real, and Val Verde Counties worsened to exceptional drought category (Stage D4), Kinney, Medina, and Uvalde to extreme (Stage D3), and Blanco, Comal, De Witt, Frio, Karnes, and Zavala to severe (Stage D2). The rest of the area remained unchanged with Bandera, Burnet, Gillespie, and Llano Counties in Stage D3 and Kendall County in Stage D2. Fire danger was moderate to high across the area at the end of April. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Kendall, Kerr, Llano, Uvalde, and Val Verde had burn bans in effect. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio, Medina, Nueces, Colorado, San Antonio, and Guadalupe River basins. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad dropped to near 42 feet below normal and Lake Travis dropped slightly to near 55 feet below normal. Medina Lake was again the most affected at 91 feet below. The Edwards Aquifer dropped again during the month and was 29.7 feet below normal, and 21 feet below the level at the end of April 2013. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in stage 2 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Uvalde was in stage 5 water restrictions, Fredericksburg moved back into stage 4 (an improvement), New Braunfels was in stage 3, and Kerrville remained in stage 1.

All but a very small portion of South Central Texas experienced below normal rainfall in April. Across most of the western half of the area they received less than 25 percent of normal for the month. With the lack of rainfall Edwards, Kerr, Real, and Val Verde Counties worsened to exceptional drought category (Stage D4), Kinney, Medina, and Uvalde to extreme (Stage D3), and Blanco, Comal, De Witt, Frio, Karnes, and Zavala to severe (Stage D2). The rest of the area remained unchanged with Bandera, Burnet, Gillespie, and Llano Counties in Stage D3 and Kendall County in Stage D2. Fire danger was moderate to high across the area at the end of April. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Kendall, Kerr, Llano, Uvalde, and Val Verde had burn bans in effect. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were much below normal (less than 10 percent) across the Frio, Medina, Nueces, Colorado, San Antonio, and Guadalupe River basins. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad dropped to near 42 feet below normal and Lake Travis dropped slightly to near 55 feet below normal. Medina Lake was again the most affected at 91 feet below. The Edwards Aquifer dropped again during the month and was 29.7 feet below normal, and 21 feet below the level at the end of April 2013. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in stage 2 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 30%. Uvalde was in stage 5 water restrictions, Fredericksburg moved back into stage 4 (an improvement), New Braunfels was in stage 3, and Kerrville remained in stage 1.

The Malone wildfire in rural northwestern Val Verde County started on April 27 (estimated around noon) and spread under breezy, dry conditions. A Red Flag Warning was in effect at the time the fire started. The fire burned into May and at the end of April had consumed 12,655 acres and was 50 percent contained. According to media reports, there were some evacuations in Pandale.

Most of South Central Texas received above normal rainfall in May. A portion of the western counties had less than normal, but mainly between 50 and 100 percent of normal. With the wet weather a number of counties had improved drought conditions. The Edwards Aquifer Authority declared stage 3 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 35%. Uvalde remained in stage 5 water restrictions, Fredericksburg improved to stage 3, and Kerrville remained in stage 1.

Lightning from a thunderstorm struck a house causing a fire. There was smoke damage to the kitchen.
A thunderstorm produced a funnel cloud which remained above the ground.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 40 mph that knocked down some tree limbs.
A thunderstorm produced a wind gust measured by a spotter at 62 mph. No damage was reported.
A thunderstorm produced hail that covered the ground. The largest hail was one inch.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 50 to 60 mph by a trained observer. No damage was reported.
A thunderstorm produced one inch hail. People were moving their vehicles under carports to protect them from the hail.
A thunderstorm produced half dollar size hail and wind gusts estimated at 55 mph.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 70 mph that blew the roof off an 80x200 foot section of an office building at the Continental Tires Test Track.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 50 mph that blew down a 6-8 inch diameter tree and multiple full trash cans.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that blew down the top half of a large, healthy Pecan tree.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing County Road 1353 south of Karnes City.
A thunderstorm produced quarter size hail. There was also very heavy rain with 1.00 inch in 45 minutes.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding. Bell Springs Rd. at Barton Creek was closed with 0.75 feet of water over the road.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding. Eight roads in New Braunfels were closed due to flooding.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding. The emergency manager reported that most low water crossings around San Marcos were closed due to flooding.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing FM 1021 in Eagle Pass and US Highway 277 near Elm Creek.
A thunderstorm produced a funnel cloud on Popebend Rd. in Cedar Creek.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding. FM187 was closed due to a flooded low water crossing.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing Whartons Dock Rd.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding. Flood waters, filled with debris, closed numerous roads in Medina.
A thunderstorm produced a wind gust measured at 61 kts by the ASOS at Pleasanton Municipal Airport.

A thunderstorm produced strong wind gusts estimated to be over 60 mph that blew over three recreational vehicles. One of the RVs was destroyed at the RV park on the north side of Yorktown.  Other Areas of Yorktown sustained quite a bit of tree damage.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing Old Mill Creed Rd. at the Sabinal River crossing.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding along Huebner Creek in San Antonio. Several low water crossings were closed due water over the road.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing many low water crossings in eastern Travis County.

A small, weak tornado touched down along County Road 242, McDonald Ln. E., and generally toward the east producing EF0 damage to a home at the corner of Martins Crossing Dr. and Single Oak Crossing. There was damage to several fences and the roof and chimney of one house. Winds were estimated to be 80 mph.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 40 mph that knocked down some tree limbs.

The Malone Fire in northwestern Val Verde County was brought under control on May 9. The fire began April 27 and eventually burned 14,587 acres and destroyed two structures. The news media reported that fire crews were able to successfully defend other structures on several ranch residences in the area. Residents of Pandale were forced to evacuate, but no damage was reported.
Several roads were closed across the south and north sides of San Antonio including the lower level of Interstate 35.

A 3 year old girl downed after being swept into a small flooded creek.  The girl went missing around 5 pm and her body was recovered shortly before midnight approximately 50-75 yards downstream.  A 5 year old was successfully rescued and recovered from his near drowning.

A NWS storm survey concluded that a microburst, associated with a severe thunderstorm, brought wind damage to the area just west of Jourdanton.  Damage included trees down, roof damage, and several pieces of irrigation equipment flipped on their sides.

June brought beneficial rain to much of South Central Texas with the Rio Grande Plains experiencing a near record rainfall event near the end of the month. With the wet weather, no county worsened during the month and Val Verde (Extreme Category (D3)), Bandera, Edwards, Kerr, Llano, and Medina (all Severe (D2)) Counties improved. The rest of the area that was in category D2 or worse remained unchanged with Gillespie County in Stage D3 and Kendall County in Stage D2. Fire danger was moderate to high across the area at the end of June. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Kerr and Val Verde had burn bans in effect. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were much below normal (less than 10 percent) for the Lower Colorado and Upper Guadalupe River Basins and below normal (10-24 percent) for the Lower Guadalupe River Basin. Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. With the extreme rain event on the 20th-21st, Lake Amistad rose close to three feet, but was still 41.6 feet below normal. Lake Travis remained 52 feet below normal. After rising slightly in May, Medina Lake dropped again and was 85 feet below normal. The Edwards Aquifer dropped during the month and was 27.6 feet below normal, and 8.1 feet below the level at the end of June 2013. The Edwards Aquifer Authority remained in stage 3 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 35%. Fredericksburg remained in stage 3 water restrictions, Kerrville in stage 1, and Del Rio entered stage 1.

A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 58 mph that blew trees down onto power lines causing numerous blackouts.
Thunderstorms produced 1.90 inches of rain in one hour which caused street flooding around Loop 1604 and I-10 in San Antonio.
A thunderstorm produced one inch hail and estimated wind gusts of 40 mph that caused some tree damage.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 to 70 mph that downed several good size trees and limbs up to six inches in diameter.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 50 mph that blew the top off a weak Cedar Elm tree and downed several six inch diameter branches.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated between 60 and 70 mph that blew the tops off of portions of barns and horse stalls.
Several funnel clouds were spotted out of thunderstorms in Uvalde County.
Thunderstorms produced wind gusts estimated at 75 mph that peeled back a portion of a metal roof, blew over a 10 inch Cedar Elm, and tore 10 inch diameter branches off trees.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that downed numerous trees and damaged one house off Highway 1174 near Joppa.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 65 mph that blew down a wood privacy fence, a large Arizona Ash, a large Red Oak, and many six inch diameter tree branches.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts measured at 66 mph.
Several funnel clouds were observed from thunderstorms in Travis County.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 80 mph that blew 20 percent of the composition shingles off the roof of a house.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 75 mph that blew the roof off of a house.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 70 mph that damaged several roofs and blew down many large trees.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that knocked down numerous trees and rows of fences.

A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated of at least 85 mph that tore the roofs off of two houses, blew the front porch of a house into another yard, and blew very large trees down onto houses. Debris was found several streets away.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that damaged a 40 year old Cedar Elm and tore six inch diameter branches off of Oaks.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that tore five inch diameter  branches off of some Lace Bark Elms.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 70 mph that caused major damage to a warehouse near Seguin.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that blew over several very large trees.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 70 mph snapped and uprooted multiple large trees and blew a wood fence approximately 30 yards.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 65 mph that uprooted large trees, snapped four inch diameter tree limbs, and damaged the roof of a barn.
A thunderstorm produced a microburst with wind speeds estimated at 60 mph. This microburst moved 300 lb. patio furniture, potted plants, and large shrubs all in different directions.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that blew down an eight inch diameter China Berry, a five inch diameter Elm, and many tree limbs.
Thunderstorms produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that blew down numerous trees and power lines between Kyle, Buda, and Dripping Springs.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that blew trees onto power lines causing power outages.
A thunderstorm produced a tornado that produced EF0 damage. The tornado touched down near County Road 208 and caused damage to some hardwood trees with estimated maximum winds of 75 mph.

A thunderstorm produced a tornado that caused EF2 damage near Shady Grove. The tornado initially touched down north of FM 963 near Bar D Trail. It damaged a wind mill, a metal barn, and uprooted numerous trees. A single family house lost numerous Spanish style tile shingles from its roof. This damage was rated EF1. The tornado then moved to the southwest where there was EF2 damage to a house to the east of FM 1174 about 0.5 miles south of the intersection with FM 963. This house was moved off of its foundation about 100 yards to the south-southwest. Five people in the house sheltered in the bathroom and had only minor cuts and scrapes. The tornado then caused tree damage on the west side of FM 1174 before lifting. Maximum winds were estimated at 125 mph.

A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 to 70 mph that downed numerous trees, power poles, damaged a grain silo north of Uvalde, overturned several train cars in Uvalde, overturned some airplanes at the Uvalde Airport, and caused power outages.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding in and around Quemado. Houses were flooded in Quemado and FM 1908 east of the town was closed due to flooding.  In the Quemado area, 1 house had major damage while 35 others reported minor damage. Similar numbers were reported around the Elm Creek area. The State of Texas reported that over 60 tons of debris was removed out of the Quemado and Elm Creek subdivisions.  Some roads remained closed for days while repairs were made.  Total estimates of loss are over 1 million dollars with regards to home and road repair, along with debris removal efforts.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing several highways in Kinney County.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding. In Del Rio, the intersection of Industrial Blvd. and Ciengas Rd. was closed as was the intersection of Farley and Las Vacas Sts. The Del Rio International Airport reported 4.67 inches of rain during this event.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding. Some people in Brackettville and Fort Clark were evacuated from their homes due to flooding. A CoCoRAHS observer five miles west of Brackettville reported 11.86 inches of rain.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing Old O'Connor Rd at Lookout Rd.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing the lower level of I-35 at San Pedro Ave.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing I-35 at Toepperwein Rd. and the ramp from eastbound I-410 to southbound I-35.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing Verbena Rd. at Southwell Rd.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing Leslie Rd. at Braun Rd.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding closing Lockhill Rd. at White Bonnet St.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding. In Pleasanton there were six to eight vehicles stranded with water up to the headlights and several roads, including Highway 281, closed with water two and a half feet deep in some places.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding filling Dry Short Prong Creek with several inches of fast flowing water. There was also one foot of water covering the main entrance to Prade Ranch and two to four feet of water flowing over two other low water crossings nearby.
Vega Verde road was flooded for several hours with portions of the road underwater.

Coop Observer reported roads flooded around Langtry.  Portions of the Judge Roy Bean Visitor Center sustained heavy water damage from a leaking roof after getting nearly 12 inches of rain in only a few hours.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that blew a metal storage building into power lines and knocked down the power poles on Tolle Rd. near Steele High School in Cibolo.

The South Central Texas counties that most needed rain generally didn���t get it in July. Most of the area that was in Severe Drought Category (D2) or worse at the beginning of the month had 75 percent of normal rainfall or less in July. This meant that Blanco County worsened to Stage D2 joining Bandera, Edwards, Kendall, Kerr, Llano, and Medina Counties. Gillespie and Val Verde Counties remained in Extreme Category (D3). Fire danger was moderate to high across the area at the end of July.  Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Kerr and Val Verde had burn bans remaining in effect and Blanco, Kendall, Llano, and Medina Counties instituted them during the month. The Texas Crop and Weather Report issued by Texas A&M Agricultural indicated hot and dry weather continued to decrease topsoil and subsoil moisture. Pasture and forage grasses were suffering from moisture stress. Hay fields were no longer growing, and after the first cutting, hay grazer fields needed rain to make a second cutting. Livestock remained in fair condition. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were below normal (10-24 percent) for the Guadalupe, Upper San Antonio, and Upper Colorado River basins. |Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad was 41.8 feet below normal. Lake Travis dropped nearly two feet to 54 feet below normal. Medina Lake dropped again and was 86 feet below normal. The Edwards Aquifer dropped during the month and was at 633.8 feet which was 5.1 feet lower than the beginning of the month and 7.6 feet below the level at the end of July 2013. The Edwards Aquifer Authority declared stage 4 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 40%. Fredericksburg remained in stage 3 water restrictions, Kerrville moved into stage 2, and Del Rio remained in stage 1.

A thunderstorm produced wind gusts estimated at 60 mph that knocked down several trees near Holbrook Rd. and Loop 410 in San Antonio.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding. A low water crossing on Ranch Rd. 783 had approximately 1.5 feet of water over the roadway between Doss and Harper.

Three children, two boys and a girl, were struck by lightning during a soccer practice at the Field of Dreams near Highway 71 and Hamilton Pool Rd. They were all taken to a hospital and all survived. One of the boys was nine years old and had serious injuries. The ages of the other two were not reported.

August was another mainly dry month for South Central Texas. Most of the region had below normal precipitation and much of that area had 50 percent or less than normal. As a result Bandera, Kendall, Kerr, and Medina Counties worsened to extreme drought category (Stage D3) and Bastrop, Bexar, Burnet, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Guadalupe, Hays, Real, and Travis moved into severe category (Stage D2). Gillespie and Val Verde remained in Stage D3 while Blanco, Edwards, and Llano continued in Stage D2. Fire danger was moderate to high across the area at the end of August.  Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Blanco, Kendall, Kerr, Llano, Medina, and Val Verde had burn bans remaining in effect and Bexar, Burnet, Caldwell, Comal, De Witt, Guadalupe, Hays, and Travis Counties instituted them during the month. The seven day stream flow averages at the end of the month were below normal (10-24 percent) for the Upper San Antonio, Upper Colorado, Medina, and Frio River basins. The Lower Colorado and Guadalupe River Basins were much below normal (less than 10 percent). Area lakes and reservoirs continued well below normal pool elevations. Lake Amistad was 41.6 feet below normal. Lake Travis dropped more than three feet to 57.4 feet below normal. Medina Lake dropped again and was 87.1 feet below normal. The Edwards Aquifer dropped during the month and was at 626.4 feet which was 2.5 feet lower than the beginning of the month and 5.1 feet below the level at the end of August 2013. The Edwards Aquifer Authority continued stage 4 water restrictions requiring large water users to reduce pumping by 40%. The Barton Springs Edwards Aquifer Conservation District declared stage 2 alarm drought status requiring a 20% reduction in pumping. San Marcos was in stage 4 water restrictions, Fredericksburg and New Braunfels were in stage 3, Kerrville, San Antonio Water System (SAWS), and Austin were in stage 2, and Del Rio and Seguin were in stage 1.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding requiring a swift water rescue at Fritz Hughes Park. A Travis County Sheriffs Deputy was reported missing around 1 AM after she called in by radio that her patrol car was being swept away by fast moving water. The 35 year old Deputy had been on patrol checking a low water crossing near the 3400 block of Fritz Hughes Park Road near Lake Austin. Her car was recovered on Thursday and her body was finally found Friday afternoon. Lower Colorado River Authority Rain gauge network reported rains in the area that totaled nearly 4 inches in 30 minutes.
